notes: In Custodia Legis, the blog of the Law Librarians of Congress; post by Margaret Wood quoting Einstein's letter to President Roosevelt.

title: Letter from Albert Einstein to U.S. President Roosevelt on the Prospect of an Atomic Bomb (August 2, 1939)
institution: German History in Documents and Images (German Historical Institute Washington)
notes: German History in Documents and Images (GHDI), an initiative of the German Historical Institute Washington DC: full transcription of the letter; the page names its source as the FDR Library (fdrlibrary.marist.edu docsworldwar.pdf). Unregistered publisher, so secondary.

title: Einstein: Image and Impact - In Brief
notes: American Institute of Physics, Center for History of Physics online exhibit. The IAS page EIN-S-0008 says it is based on this exhibit, so the two pages share one origin text (not independent in content). Unregistered publisher (proposal in data/registry/PROPOSED.md), so secondary.

title: Famed scientist at work for U.S. Navy
notes: LoC Prints and Photographs item record (BIOG FILE). Same occasion as NARA 80-G-42919 (EIN-S-0029). Rights advisory 'Rights status not evaluated', so the LoC copy is not staged as media.

claim: Now it appears almost certain that this could be achieved in the immediate future.

evidence.quote: Now it appears almost certain that this could be achieved in the immediate future.
evidence.locator: post body, paragraph 3 (quoted from the letter)

evidence.quote: Between July 18 and August 15, 1939, one of the most consequential letters in modern history was drafted by Albert Einstein and the Hungarian-born physicist Leo Szilard
Now it appears almost certain that this could be achieved in the immediate future.
Letter from Albert Einstein to U.S. President Roosevelt on the Prospect of an Atomic Bomb (August 2, 1939)

notes: Sentence from Einstein's letter of 2 August 1939 to President F. D. Roosevelt (the original is in the FDR Library, NARA; NAID 16608874 file unit 'Sachs, Alexander', scan only, no transcription in the catalog). The LoC post says the letter was drafted by Einstein and Leo Szilard; it was signed by Einstein. Context: 'this' refers to setting up a nuclear chain reaction in a large mass of uranium (previous sentence of the letter).

claim: However such bombs might very well prove to be too heavy for transportation by air.

evidence.quote: However such bombs might very well prove to be too heavy for transportation by air.
evidence.locator: post body, paragraph 4 (quoted from the letter)

evidence.quote: Between July 18 and August 15, 1939, one of the most consequential letters in modern history was drafted by Albert Einstein and the Hungarian-born physicist Leo Szilard
However, such bombs might very well prove to be too heavy for transportation by air.
Letter from Albert Einstein to U.S. President Roosevelt on the Prospect of an Atomic Bomb (August 2, 1939)

notes: Sentence from Einstein's letter of 2 August 1939 to President F. D. Roosevelt. The LoC post prints it without the comma after 'However'; the GHDI transcription has 'However, such bombs'. The claim follows the registry-institutional source (LoC). Drafted by Einstein and Leo Szilard per the LoC post.

claim: How I wish that somewhere there existed an island for those who are wise and of goodwill! In such a place even I would be an ardent patriot.

evidence.quote: How I wish that somewhere there existed an island for those who are wise and of goodwill! In such a place even I would be an ardent patriot.
How I wish that somewhere there existed an island for those who are wise and of goodwill! In such a place even I would be an ardent patriot.

notes: Pull quote in the Einstein life timeline of the IAS page and of the AIP exhibit it is based on; neither page names the document or date it comes from. Attribution to Einstein is by the pages' context (quotes of Einstein in an Einstein exhibit). The two pages share one origin text, so the corroboration is weaker than two independent holders.

claim: One thing I have learned in a long life: that all our science, measured against reality, is primitive and childlike—and yet it is the most precious thing we have.

evidence.quote: One thing I have learned in a long life: that all our science, measured against reality, is primitive and childlike—and yet it is the most precious thing we have.

notes: Closing pull quote of the IAS 'In Brief' timeline and of the AIP exhibit it is based on (AIP prints a spaced en dash where IAS has an em dash). Neither page names the source document or date. The two pages share one origin text.

Dr. Albert Einstein, who is doing research for the Bureau of Ordnance, in his study at Princeton, N.J.

notes: Ties the 24 July 1943 Navy photographs (EIN-M-0013, EIN-M-0014) to the study in his home. LoC's record notes 'This record contains unverified data from caption card.'
